0.title: What Are You Living For?
0.essay:
Not everyone goes to church, but everyone worships. Every human heart bows to something. It may be a career, a family, a body, a bank balance, a cause, or simply being liked. The question is never whether we worship, but what. This study is about the false gods of the heart, and how to become a true worshipper of the living God.

An old word for a modern heart

Idolatry sounds ancient: carved statues, smoky temples, people bowing to wood and stone. Most of us have never been tempted to kneel before a golden calf. But the Bible says idols live first in the heart, and only sometimes on a shelf. An idol is whatever we look to for the life, safety, worth and joy that only God can give. By that measure, idols are as common in a modern city as they were in ancient Athens.

So this is not a study about other people. Every one of us has been, and in some measure still is, a worshipper of things that cannot save.

Not to shame, but to free

To talk about idols can sound harsh. But God exposes our idols the way a doctor names an illness: in order to heal it. Idols are cruel masters. They promise everything and enslave us. God’s purpose in uncovering them is to bring us home to the one who made us, loves us and gave himself for us. The goal of this study is not that you would love fewer things, but that you would love God most, and everything else in its right place.

The chapters

Everyone Worships; Good Things Made Ultimate; Finding Your Idols; What Idols Promise and What They Do; The Expulsive Power of a Greater Love; and Becoming a Worshipper.

For reflection

If someone watched your life for a month, without hearing anything you say you believe, what would they conclude you live for?

1.title: Everyone Worships
1.essay:
We tend to think of idolatry as something that belongs to other times and places. The Bible will not let us off so lightly. It says that human beings never stop worshipping. We only change what we worship.

The great exchange

Paul describes the whole human race in Romans 1. “For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened” (Romans 1:21). Then comes a key word: they “exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen” (Romans 1:25).

Notice the word exchanged. People did not stop worshipping when they turned from God. They swapped one object for another. The capacity to adore, trust and serve was still there. It was simply pointed at created things. And notice where it began: they would not honour God or give him thanks. Ingratitude is the soil in which idols grow. When we stop receiving life as a gift from God, we start demanding it from something else.

We were made to worship. God made us to know him, love him and enjoy him, and a heart made for God will not stay empty. If it does not rest on him, it will lean its whole weight on something smaller. Augustine of Hippo put it in a famous prayer: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

Idols in the heart

In Ezekiel’s day some elders of Israel came to sit before the prophet, wanting a word from God. They looked respectable. They carried no statues. But God said to Ezekiel, “Son of man, these men have taken their idols into their hearts, and set the stumbling block of their iniquity before their faces” (Ezekiel 14:3).

That is a searching sentence. An idol can be carried into a prayer meeting. It can sit in a pew. You can hold one while singing a hymn. The idol is not first a thing in the hand but a love in the heart, something we set “before” our faces, so that we see everything else through it.

Yet look at God’s purpose in exposing these men: “that I may lay hold of the hearts of the house of Israel, who are all estranged from me through their idols” (Ezekiel 14:5). God is not only angry at idolatry. He wants his people’s hearts back.

Greed is idolatry

The New Testament carries the same idea into ordinary life. Writing to Christians, Paul says, “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5). Covetousness is wanting something so much that it begins to rule you. Paul calls that idolatry, not because the greedy person bows to a statue, but because money or possessions have taken the place in the heart that belongs to God. He says the same in Ephesians, where the covetous person is “(that is, an idolater)” (Ephesians 5:5).

Jesus said the same thing plainly: “You cannot serve God and money” (Matthew 6:24). Money is not evil. But it can become a master.

Believing and bowing

Idolatry is not only a problem for unbelievers. After the northern kingdom of Israel fell, the people settled in the land tried to keep both. “So these nations feared the LORD and also served their carved images” (2 Kings 17:41). They added the Lord to their gods without letting him replace them.

Churchgoing people can do exactly this. We can sing about Christ on Sunday and look to our career, our reputation or our children for our real security on Monday. John Calvin called the human heart a perpetual factory of idols: we do not need to be taught to make them. Martin Luther, explaining the first commandment, said in effect that whatever your heart clings to and relies on is really your god. That is a test we can all apply.

An example

A retired man, a faithful church member for forty years, smiles at the idea that he might have idols. Then a downturn in the markets cuts his savings sharply. He cannot sleep. He checks the figures many times a day and snaps at his wife. One night he admits to himself that he has prayed about it far less than he has worried about it. He believes in God. But he has been resting on his savings.

The rescuer speaks first

There is hope in all this, and it lies in the order of God’s words at Sinai. Before he said, “You shall have no other gods before me,” he said, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2–3). The command not to have other gods comes from the God who has already rescued his people. He does not ask for our worship as a tyrant, but as a Saviour. Every idol is a return to the house of slavery. God calls us out of it, to himself.

For reflection

Where do you see the “great exchange” of Romans 1 in the world around you? Where do you see it in yourself? Why do you think ingratitude and idolatry go together? If whatever your heart clings to is your god, what would that test reveal about you this week?

2.title: Good Things Made Ultimate
2.essay:
Most idols do not look like idols. Very few people worship things they know to be evil. We worship good things: love, family, work, health, success, even ministry. That is what makes idols so hard to see, and so hard to let go.

What an idol is

Timothy Keller’s book Counterfeit Gods is one of the clearest modern treatments of this subject. He defined an idol as “anything more important to you than God, anything that absorbs your heart and imagination more than God, anything you seek to give you what only God can give.”

Keller often pointed out that the problem with idols is rarely the thing itself. An idol is usually a good thing turned into an ultimate thing. And the better the thing is, the more likely we are to expect it to meet our deepest needs. A career is good. A marriage is good. Children are a blessing from God. But when any of these becomes the place where we look for our worth, our safety or our meaning, it has been given a weight it was never designed to carry.

Jacob and the morning after

Genesis tells of a man who poured all his hopes into one person. Jacob loved Rachel so much that he worked seven years to marry her, “and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her” (Genesis 29:20). Rachel was not wrong to love, nor was Jacob wrong to love her. But he seems to have looked to her for everything. Then, after the wedding, comes one of the saddest lines in Genesis: “And in the morning, behold, it was Leah!” (Genesis 29:25).

Keller drew attention to this verse in Counterfeit Gods. Jacob had been deceived by Laban, but there is a deeper lesson. Whatever we make ultimate will, in the end, disappoint us like that. We go to bed with our dream and wake up to something finite. Even when we get exactly what we wanted, it cannot be God for us.

The story has a tender twist. Leah, unloved, named her first sons in the hope that her husband would love her at last. Then, with her fourth son, she said, “This time I will praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:35), and called him Judah. From Judah came the line of kings, and in the end Jesus Christ. The woman who stopped looking to a husband for what only God could give became an ancestor of the Saviour.

Abraham and the gift

Abraham waited decades for the son God had promised. Then God said, “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love” (Genesis 22:2), and told him to offer him up. It is a hard chapter, and God stopped Abraham’s hand. But it shows that God watches the gifts he gives, lest they take his place. The angel said, “now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me” (Genesis 22:12). Abraham was not asked to love Isaac less. He was asked to love God more. And the God who spared Abraham’s son would one day not spare his own.

Surface idols and deep idols

It helps to see that idols often come in layers. On the surface are things we can name: money, a relationship, a career, a home, a body shape, a child’s achievements. Underneath them are deeper longings that these things are serving. Keller, drawing on other Christian counsellors, often spoke of four of these deep idols: approval, control, comfort and power.

Two people can chase the same surface idol for different reasons. One works long hours because success brings admiration (approval). Another works the same hours because money feels like safety (control). A third wants an easy life with no pain or pressure (comfort). A fourth wants to be on top and to have influence (power). Asking “What is this really giving me?” helps us see what lies beneath. Other studies in this commentary look closely at some of these: The Fear of Man on approval, Control and Trust on control, Humility & Pride on power, and Envy & Comparison on wanting what others have.

Religious idols

Some of the most stubborn idols are religious. We can make an idol of our moral record, our correct doctrine, our church’s growth, our spiritual gifts or our reputation for godliness. Then we are trusting our own goodness rather than God’s grace, and the gospel itself has been quietly replaced. The Pharisees were not irreligious men. They had made their religion into a way of being their own saviours.

An example

A mother has given her life to her children, and loves them dearly. When her son leaves university without finishing, she is not only sad for him. She feels as if her own life has failed. For weeks she cannot pray. Slowly she sees that her children’s success had become her proof that she was a good person. She had loved them well, but she had also needed them to justify her. Seeing it hurts. It also frees her to love her son as he is.

Not less love, but ordered love

The answer to idolatry is not to love good things less. Augustine spoke of rightly ordered loves: loving each thing according to its true worth, and God above all. When God is first, a husband can love his wife without crushing her under the demand to be his saviour. A worker can do excellent work without being destroyed by failure. Idols actually harm the things we idolise, because we ask them to be what they cannot be. Putting God first is good for them too.

For reflection

Which good things in your life might have become ultimate things? Have you ever had a “morning after” like Jacob’s, when something you longed for turned out to be less than you hoped? Of approval, control, comfort and power, which pulls at you most? What would it look like to love that good thing in its right place?

3.title: Finding Your Idols
3.essay:
Idols hide. No one says, “My reputation is my god.” We call our idols prudence, ambition, love for family, or simply “how things are”. So we need some honest questions, and the help of the God who sees the heart.

A heart that deceives

“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). We are skilled at hiding our motives, even from ourselves. That is why idols are rarely found by asking, “Do I have any idols?” The answer is almost always no. They are found by looking at the evidence of our lives.

In Counterfeit Gods Keller suggested a number of questions for this, and pastors through the centuries have used similar ones. Here are some of the most useful.

Where does your mind go when it is free?

What do you daydream about? When you are in the shower, driving, or lying awake, what does your imagination drift towards? It may be a future success, a relationship, a house, being admired, or getting even. What we enjoy thinking about when nothing else demands our attention often shows what we treasure. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

Where do your money and time go?

Look at your bank statements and your calendar. They tell an honest story. We spend freely on what we love and are careful, even mean, with what we do not. This does not mean every large expense is an idol. But if you give generously to your hobby and grudgingly to God’s work, or if your diary always has room for work and never for prayer, the pattern is worth noticing. Jesus warned, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15).

What could you not bear to lose?

Finish the sentence, “If I lost ______, I would have no reason to go on.” Whatever fills that blank honestly may be functioning as your god. A rich man once ran up to Jesus, eager to know how to inherit eternal life. Jesus looked at him and loved him, and named the one thing: “go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Mark 10:21). “Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions” (Mark 10:22). He could keep the commandments. He could not let go of his wealth.

Jesus does not ask everyone to sell everything. But he did put his finger on the one thing that man could not surrender, and he may do the same with us.

What makes you most anxious, angry or despairing?

Our strongest emotions are often like smoke alarms. Keller often made the point that when an idol is threatened we become anxious, when it is blocked we become angry, and when it is lost we fall into despair. Of course not every fear or anger comes from an idol. But if a small threat to something sends you into panic or rage out of all proportion, ask what that thing has come to mean to you. The studies Anger and Contentment & Anxiety look at these emotions more fully.

What would you do wrong to get or keep?

Another clue: what would you be tempted to lie, cheat, neglect people or break a promise for? We are willing to sin for our gods. If you notice that you will cut corners for one thing in particular, that thing has a hold on you.

Ask God, and ask friends

Because the heart deceives, we need help to see it. Pray David’s prayer: “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!” (Psalm 139:23–24). Then ask a spouse or a trusted friend, “What do you think I live for?” Their answer may surprise you. This is part of what the church is for: “exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13).

An example

A young man in sales is furious when a colleague gets the promotion he wanted. At first he tells himself it is about fairness. But as he works through these questions he notices other things. He daydreams about being the one people look up to. He spends heavily on clothes and a car he cannot really afford. He is anxious whenever a friend seems to be doing better. Slowly he sees that his god is not money or even work, but being somebody. That is painful to see. It is also the first honest prayer he has prayed in months.

Searching without spiralling

This kind of self-examination can go wrong. Some people turn it into an endless inward search, picking over every motive and never feeling clean. That is not what God intends. The Scottish minister Robert Murray M’Cheyne counselled taking ten looks at Christ for every look at yourself. The aim of finding an idol is not to stare at it, but to turn from it to him.

If you find that examining your heart becomes compulsive, so that you cannot stop checking your thoughts and motives, or you are tormented by fears that you have sinned unforgivably, please speak to your pastor and to a doctor. This can be a form of anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder, and good help is available. Getting it is not a failure of faith.

For reflection

Which of these questions was the hardest to answer honestly? What does your imagination drift towards when it is free? What strong emotion have you felt recently that might be pointing to something you treasure too much? Who could you ask, “What do you think I live for?”

4.title: What Idols Promise and What They Do
4.essay:
Every idol makes a promise. “Have me, and you will be safe.” “Have me, and you will matter.” “Have me, and you will be free.” Idols are persuasive because their promises sound like life. But they never keep them.

Broken cisterns

Through Jeremiah, God describes his people’s idolatry in one picture: “for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

A fountain is a spring that flows freely, fresh and endless. A cistern is a pit cut out of rock to catch rainwater. It is hard work to dig, and even when it is finished its water is stale. These cisterns are also cracked. The people turned from a free spring to back-breaking labour for something that leaks away. That is what every idol is like. It costs a great deal and holds nothing.

Isaiah asks the same question: “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?” (Isaiah 55:2). Think of the person who gets the job, the house, the relationship or the recognition they longed for, and finds that the ache is still there.

You become what you worship

Psalm 115 mocks the idols of the nations: “They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see. They have ears, but do not hear” (Psalm 115:5–6). Then comes the warning: “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8).

We are shaped by what we worship. Jeremiah says the same: “they went far from me, and went after worthlessness, and became worthless” (Jeremiah 2:5). A person who worships money tends to become hard and cold, like metal. A person who worships approval becomes hollow, changing shape to fit every crowd. A person who worships control becomes rigid and fearful. A person who worships comfort becomes small. The idol not only fails to give life. It drains life from us.

From servant to master

Idols begin as servants. We use them to get what we want. But they soon become masters. Paul reminded the Galatians, “Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods” (Galatians 4:8). The more we serve an idol, the more it demands. The shopping, the drinking, the work, the screen, the need to be noticed: each asks for a little more each time, and gives a little less. “The sorrows of those who run after another god shall multiply” (Psalm 16:4).

Isaiah has a striking picture. When Babylon fell, its gods had to be loaded on to animals and carried away. “Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts” (Isaiah 46:1). Then God speaks to his people: “even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:4). There is the difference. You have to carry your idols. The living God carries you.

The lie in the right hand

Isaiah 44 describes a man who cuts down a tree, burns half of it to cook his dinner and warm himself, and then carves the rest into a god and bows down to it. It would be funny if it were not so tragic. “He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray” (Isaiah 44:20). He cannot step back far enough to ask whether the thing he is holding is a lie. Idolatry blinds us. That is why the false promise keeps working on us even after it has failed many times.

Idols cannot forgive

There is one more thing idols cannot do. Timothy Keller often pointed out that if you live for your career and you fail, your career will not forgive you; it will punish you. If you live for your appearance, it will mock you as you age. Only Jesus is a Lord who, if you fail him, will forgive you. Idols are merciless because they are not persons who love us. Jonah, praying from the depths, saw it clearly: “Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love” (Jonah 2:8). To hold on to an idol is to let go of the one thing it can never give: steadfast love.

An example

A woman is admired by everyone for her beautiful home and her generous hospitality. But no gathering is ever good enough for her. She is exhausted before guests arrive and resentful while they are there. One evening, after a dinner she thought went badly, she bursts into tears and cannot say why. Later, with a friend, she sees it. Her home had become her way of proving her worth. It had promised her that if everything was perfect, she would finally feel enough. It never once delivered.

The mercy of a fallen idol

Sometimes God lets our idols fall. When the Philistines captured the ark of God and put it in the temple of their god Dagon, they came in the next morning and “behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD” (1 Samuel 5:3). Their response is very human: “they took Dagon and put him back in his place” (1 Samuel 5:3). We often do the same. A loss, a failure or a disappointment knocks something off its throne, and we rush to set it up again.

But a fallen idol can be a mercy. It may be God’s way of calling us home. If the loss of something you loved has left you in deep darkness, do not carry it alone. Speak to your pastor and friends. If low mood persists, see a doctor: depression is an illness, and treatment, including medicine, is no failure of faith. The study Depression & the Christian says more. And if you are having thoughts of ending your life, please get help now: call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust.

For reflection

What broken cistern have you worked hard to dig? In what ways have you seen yourself “become like” something you have trusted too much? Which idols in your life feel like burdens you have to carry? What would it mean to be carried by God instead?

5.title: The Expulsive Power of a Greater Love
5.essay:
Once we see an idol, our first instinct is to get rid of it. We try harder, make rules, promise ourselves we will stop. Sometimes that helps for a while. But an idol cannot simply be removed. It has to be replaced by something we love more.

The empty house

Jesus told a strange story about an unclean spirit that leaves a person and then returns, “and when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order” (Matthew 12:44). So it brings seven others, “and the last state of that person is worse than the first” (Matthew 12:45). Jesus was speaking about his own generation, but the picture fits the human heart. A heart that is cleaned up but left empty will not stay empty. Moral effort alone can sweep the house. It cannot fill it.

A new affection

The Scottish minister Thomas Chalmers (1780–1847) preached a famous sermon called The Expulsive Power of a New Affection. He argued that the heart cannot be freed from the love of the world simply by being shown how empty the world is. It must be given something better to love. A love is driven out only by a stronger love. Timothy Keller drew on Chalmers often. He pointed out that if you only uproot an idol and do not plant the love of Christ in its place, the idol will grow back.

This is good news. It means the way out of idolatry is not grim self-denial alone. It is delight. The cure for loving the wrong things too much is to love God more, and to see that he is more lovely than anything we have put in his place.

The true fountain

Every idol is a counterfeit of something only Christ can truly give. The broken cisterns of Jeremiah 2 are answered by Jesus at a well: “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (John 4:13–14). On the great day of the feast he cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35).

Do you long for approval? In Christ the Father’s delight rests on you. For safety? He holds all things and will never let you go. For significance? You are part of his eternal kingdom. For comfort? He gives rest to the weary. What the idol promised falsely, he gives truly, and for ever. The psalmist found it: “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:25–26).

The one man with no idols

Only one human being has ever loved God with all his heart, soul, mind and strength. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus “all the kingdoms of the world and their glory” and said, “All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:8–9). It was the greatest offer any idol has ever made. Jesus answered, “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve’” (Matthew 4:10). Where Adam, Israel and every one of us have bowed, he stood. And he stood for us.

He gave himself

Here is the heart of it. The greater love that drives out our idols is not first our love for God. It is his love for us. Paul wrote, “I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Think of the difference. Every idol says, “Give me your life, and then I may bless you.” Christ says, “I have given my life for you.” Idols demand sacrifices. The living God provides the sacrifice. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). On the cross he, who had never once exchanged the glory of God for anything, bore the guilt of all our exchanges. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). He was forsaken so that idolaters could be welcomed home.

When that love is seen, idols begin to look small. Not because we have stopped wanting good things, but because we have found the one who is better than all of them, and who loved us when we were loving everything but him.

Beholding, we become

Psalm 115 warned that we become like what we worship. The gospel turns that warning into a promise. “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Where is that glory seen? “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). As we look at him, in his word, in worship, in prayer, the Spirit slowly makes us like him. One day the work will be complete: “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

God promised this through Ezekiel: “from all your idols I will cleanse you. And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:25–26). Freedom from idols is not our achievement. It is the work of the Spirit, given to all who belong to Christ.

Joy that lets go

Jesus said the kingdom is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found, “Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13:44). Note the words “in his joy”. He did not give things up grudgingly. He had found something worth more. Paul said the same: “I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8).

An example

For years a man tried to break his habit of spending far beyond his means. He made budgets and cut up cards, and always slid back. What began to change him was not a new rule. In a home group studying the generosity of Christ, he was struck by 2 Corinthians 8:9 and began, almost reluctantly, to give regularly. He found that giving brought a joy that buying never had. The pull of spending did not vanish, but it weakened. He had found a better treasure.

Keep yourselves from idols

John ends his first letter with a vision of Christ: “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). Only then does he add his final word: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21). The command follows the vision. We keep ourselves from idols by keeping our eyes on the one who is true.

For reflection

Have you tried to remove an idol by willpower alone? What happened? Which idol in your life promises something that Christ gives truly? Read Galatians 2:20 slowly. How does it change things to know that he gave himself for you? What would it look like for you to let go of something “in joy”?

6.title: Becoming a Worshipper
6.essay:
Jesus said, “the Father is seeking such people to worship him” (John 4:23). Turning from idols is only half the story. God is not merely emptying our hearts of false gods. He is making us true worshippers, people whose whole lives are turned towards him in love.

With all of life

“I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1). Worship is not only singing. It is offering your whole self, body and days, to God, in response to his mercy. Work, meals, rest, friendships and money all become ways of honouring him. “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). An idol asks to be the centre of life. Worship puts God at the centre, and everything else finds its place around him.

With God’s people

Idols grow strongest when we are alone. One of God’s great gifts against them is the gathered church on the Lord’s Day. Week by week, the preached word tells us again what is true. The songs put better words in our mouths than our hearts would choose. The Lord’s Supper sets Christ before our eyes. Fellow believers know us and encourage us. “And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together” (Hebrews 10:24–25).

When the psalmist was troubled by envy of the wicked, he could not make sense of things “until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17). Gathered worship resets our sense of what is great and what is small. The study Worship & the Lord’s Day explores what happens when the church gathers and how to keep the Lord’s Day.

In secret

David wrote, “One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple” (Psalm 27:4). Idols scatter the heart in many directions. Worship gathers it to “one thing”. In Psalm 63, written in the wilderness, David prays, “O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you” (Psalm 63:1), and then, “Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you” (Psalm 63:3).

Private worship need not be complicated. Read a passage of Scripture. Let it show you something about God. Then tell him what you see, and thank him. Praise is simply telling God what he is like. Thanksgiving is telling him what he has done. Remember that idolatry began with ingratitude (Romans 1:21). Gratitude is one of its strongest cures.

Daily habits

Here are some simple practices that help a heart turn towards God:

Begin with God. Before you check your phone, read a psalm and pray a sentence or two. You might use the prayer, “Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways” (Psalm 119:37).

Give thanks specifically. Name three gifts from God each day. Thank him as the giver, so that the gifts do not take his place.

Give something away. Regular generosity loosens the grip of money and things.

Rest. A weekly day of rest declares that your work is not your god and the world will not fall apart without you.

Review the day. In the evening ask, “Where did my heart run today? What did I look to for comfort, worth or safety?” Then bring what you find to Christ.

When an idol is exposed

Name it. Tell God plainly what you have been looking to in his place. Do not soften it.

Repent. “Repent and turn away from your idols” (Ezekiel 14:6). Repentance is more than regret at the consequences. It is turning from the idol to God. And it is safe: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Rejoice. Keller often spoke of repentance that ends not in gloom but in joy. Do not stop at sorrow. Look at Christ in the very way the idol promised to help you. If the idol was approval, rejoice that you are accepted in him. If it was control, rejoice that he reigns. Let the greater love do its work.

Take a step. Do something concrete in the opposite direction: give away what you were clinging to, step back from a role that had become your identity, tell a friend, or change a habit that feeds the idol.

Expect a fight, not defeat. Idols grow back. You will find yourself at the same cistern again. That is not proof that nothing has changed. God says to his wandering people, “O Ephraim, what have I to do with idols? It is I who answer and look after you” (Hosea 14:8). Turn again, as often as you need to.

When it is more than an idol

Some idols take the form of addictions: alcohol, drugs, gambling, pornography, food. These need more than good intentions. Please talk to your pastor, see a doctor, and look for a qualified counsellor or a recovery group. That is not a lack of faith. It is wisdom. The study Fighting Sin & Temptation has more help. If you are in despair, or having thoughts of harming yourself, get help now: call the emergency services or a crisis line, such as Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland or 988 in the United States, and tell someone you trust.

An example

A doctor in her forties realises her work has become her god. She takes three small steps. She reads a psalm before opening her emails. She keeps Sunday free, worships with her church and has lunch with friends. Each evening she asks where her heart ran that day. Some weeks she slides back. But a year later she notices she can leave the hospital and be fully at home. Work is still important. It is no longer everything.

Worship for ever

All of this is practice for eternity. In the new creation, “the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face” (Revelation 22:3–4). There will be no idols there, because there will be nothing left to want. Every true longing that drove us to false gods will be met in the face of the one who loved us and gave himself for us.

Further reading

Timothy Keller’s Counterfeit Gods is a clear and searching book on this subject. Thomas Chalmers’s sermon The Expulsive Power of a New Affection is short and still worth reading. G. K. Beale’s We Become What We Worship traces the theme through the whole Bible at greater depth. The study Love: The Greatest Commandment looks at what it means to love God with all your heart.

For reflection

Which part of worship comes least naturally to you: in all of life, with God’s people, or in private? Which daily habit could you begin this week? Is there an idol you need to name, repent of and rejoice over today? What do you most look forward to in seeing his face?
